video.title: This Ridiculously Simple Business Makes Him $4M/Year (Can’t Fail)

summary: David Heacock interviews Ian Dolberg, founder of Dolcore, a New York City (Staten Island) security guard agency started in 2018 after military service and years working for large guard firms. Revenue went from $90k in year one to about $670k, then $1.3M, then nearly $4M in 2024, dipping to $3.3M last year as client funding was cut. Ian describes cold-calling sales, shotgun hiring, regulatory barriers, thin margins (~7%) and price-driven RFP losses. He also launched a marketing agency (Black Op Digital) for other guard companies. The host pushes him on value proposition, retention and systems. Key takeaway: a people-heavy, regulated, low-margin service that grew via founder-led outbound sales and niche compliance moats, but it is not agent-automatable.

speakers.name: David Heacock

speakers.name: Ian Dolberg
speakers.description: Founder of Dolcore security guard agency, Staten Island/NYC; Coast Guard veteran

ideas.name: Dolcore security guard agency (NYC)
ideas.one_liner: Licensed security guard staffing for NYC businesses, nonprofits, schools, cannabis, residential and events.
ideas.business_model: Hourly bill rate to clients for supplied guards; margin is the markup over guard wages, insurance, uniforms and equipment.
ideas.customer: NYC businesses and institutions needing licensed guards: cannabis dispensaries, supportive housing and shelters, private schools, retail, banks, co-ops/HOAs, residential buildings, event organisers, nonprofits.
ideas.problem: Businesses need legally licensed guards reliably present; a single in-house guard calling out leaves them unprotected or unable to open, and in-house forces carry insurance and licensing burdens.
ideas.offer: Licensed, military-led guards from a pool of about 200, with callout cover, 24/7 central monitoring of guards, supervisors, SOPs, training and paperwork for prevailing-wage contracts; plus bespoke tech such as a vibe-coded gate access control system.

pricing.model: Hourly bill rate over guard wage; tiered guard experience levels; competitive bidding via RFPs

price_points.label: 24-hour guard service for first residential client
Access control system the incumbent charged a gated community

pricing.notes: Race to the bottom on bid rates; minimum wage rises push prices up and clients shop around.

acquisition_channels.details: Founder cold-called facilities managers, property managers and security directors; sent a letter and packet/trifold beforehand announcing a call time, then called; weekly batches of 10 LinkedIn-sourced contacts. Now a hired salesperson trained in his method (outbound calls and emails).
Connected with property managers on LinkedIn, pulled emails into an Excel sheet and followed up.
Paid $50 to join the Metropolitan Cemetery Association to reach cemetery directors; Staten Island Chamber of Commerce, golf committee and event sponsorships.
In-house SEO team plus Google Ads; about $135k a year on marketing; aims to respond to quote requests within 15 minutes.
Friend introductions (bank client via Statland Security owner, Snug Harbor event); guards alert him when a site gets a new security director.
Invited to many RFPs; bid about $100M in RFPs this year and won none because of price; DCAS-certified school list gives grant-funded school work.
Event videos and a guard music video on website, YouTube and social, linked in proposals instead of stock photos.

ideas.delivery: Humans physically staff posts. Dispatch runs 24 hours, central monitoring watches guards, supervisors (mostly veterans) do random night inspections. Hiring via personal network, sponsored Indeed posts and social media, with interviews at coffee shops initially.
unit_economics_claims: About 7% margin, which he says could be adjusted up to about 19%
$8k per week of revenue is roughly $400k a year, giving about $28k profit at 7%
2024 revenue just under $4M, 2025 $3.3M, projected a little over $4M this year
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (security agency licence obtained; first year funded by cold calling while employed as an investigator)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About one month after quitting, three cemetery contracts began (April 2018 start).

acquisition.how: Inbound SEO and ads can be automated, but his proven method is human phone outreach to decision makers and RFPs; cold email to limited companies is legal in the UK but calls need TPS screening.

onboarding.how: Needs licensed guards recruited, vetted, trained and placed at physical sites; contracts and site walkthroughs are mostly human.

delivery.how: Physical guarding by licensed humans; agents could only help with scheduling, monitoring and reporting.

billing.how: Hourly invoicing and payroll (including prevailing-wage paperwork) can be largely software-driven.

support.how: Callouts, guard no-shows and client complaints need a human dispatcher in real time.

uk_applicability.notes: UK equivalent exists, with Security Industry Authority licensing for guards and approved contractor scheme, Working Time/minimum wage rules and thin margins; NYC-specific laws (Security Guard Act, FO4 fire guard, DCAS, prevailing wage) do not apply. The model works with changes but is labour-heavy.

risks: Margins around 7% and commodity price competition from PE-backed consolidators
Client funding cuts and new security directors causing contract loss
High insurance costs and liability, for example nightclub premiums after the Astroworld incident
Guard callouts and the difficulty of staffing sites
Dependence on the founder for sales
Event work is lumpy and was an existential risk when staffing needs tripled

tactics.name: Letter, packet then scheduled call
steps: Identify the decision maker (facilities manager, security director, property manager)
Send a typed letter and a memorable packet or trifold announcing a specific call time
Call at that time and ask for the person as 'expecting my call'
Batch ten contacts a week, calling the following week to book meetings

quote.text: I'm going to be calling you at 10 p.m. on Wednesday and what I would do is like leave something that's memorable like a packet or a trifold
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

tactics.name: Join the niche trade association for lead access
steps: Find the niche association (cemeteries)
Pay the membership ($50)
Call every member director

quote.text: I got a hold of the Metropolitan Cemetery Association director by becoming a member for $50.
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

tactics.name: Shotgun hiring for urgent staffing
steps: Call known managers and guards first
Sponsor Indeed posts and blast social media
Interview in coffee shops
Over-hire (16 for 13 posts) to cover no-shows

quote.text: I was able to do shotgun hiring and I would blast out
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

tactics.name: Use event video as proof in proposals
steps: Hire a camera person to film the event and guards
Publish on website, YouTube and social
Link video in every proposal instead of stock photos

quote.text: whenever we do proposals, we have the link to like our near or like a music video I put together of the guards like working
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

tactics.name: Spin out your marketing function as an agency
steps: Build an in-house SEO and outbound team
Sell the service to non-competing territories
Use agency profits to fund your own marketing

quote.text: I built the marketing agency to pay for my marketing and it's worked.
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

tactics.name: New-decision-maker alert
steps: Ask guards to report any new security director at a site
Have the sales person or owner meet the new director quickly
Reassure them to reduce churn risk

steps: Document the personal call method
Hire and train a salesperson
Track results by quarter

Founder sales effort stagnated when it required 30 calls a week by himself.

lessons.lesson: Work in the industry first at large competitors to learn bill rates, P&L and sales before starting your own.

quote.text: I needed to learn about the guarding. I didn't know what bill rates were.
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

lessons.lesson: Start in niches big competitors ignore (cemeteries) to win first clients as a startup.
Regulatory barriers (licences, certification lists like DCAS) create moats and make some sales easy.

quote.text: There's a lot of regulations uh which I find barrier to entry which is good for my business
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

lessons.lesson: Founder-led sales stops scaling; teach a hire your method and use a book like Who Not How.
Commodity labour services have thin margins; diversify so no client exceeds 20% of the portfolio.

quote.text: Nothing in my portfolio takes more than 20% of my portfolio.
quote.speaker: Ian Dolberg

lessons.lesson: Retention means revenue you can count on next year, regardless of why it leaves; bake client-funding risk into the model.
A business that runs without the founder is more valuable and easier to pass on than one where the owner does everything.
A clear, sellable unique value proposition is needed in a commodity market; being military-owned and monitored guards was his differentiation but the host found it under-articulated.
Reinvest in marketing and be willing to change methods each year; word-of-mouth-only competitors stayed small.
A big early win can come with a crash afterwards; plan for repeatability and diversify.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with a coherent revenue timeline and some specifics (margin, weekly revenue, deposits), but figures are unverified, many details are vague, and the host steers into coaching. The business is a labour-heavy local service, not relevant to agent-run operation.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Ian runs Black Op Digital, a marketing agency selling to other guard companies, and the channel is a business podcast.
